Wreaths
rēthz
n. pl. (the twisted chain work covering the capitals of the temple pillars; Hebrew sarsar, gedilah)
Old English writha, a twisted band, from writhan, to twist. In the temple account the wreaths are chain work — interlaced metal cordage — not garlands of leaves.

Biblical Definition

Hiram's work on the two pillars is described in detail: “nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter” (1Ki 7:17). Chronicles counts them again with the pommels: “the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars” (2Ch 4:12), and adds the fruit: “four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath” (2Ch 4:13). Kings gives the same care to the network and its rows (1Ki 7:18). Two free-standing pillars, holding up nothing, crowned with chains and fruit at the door of the house of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a wreath as something twisted or curled; a garland or chaplet; and in architecture, ornamental work twisted or interlaced.

expand to see more

WREATH, n. Something twisted; a garland; a chaplet; as a wreath of flowers.

WREATH, n. In architecture, an ornament of twisted or interlaced work, as of chains or cords.

CHAPITER, n. The upper part or capital of a column or pillar.

Key Scripture

1Ki 7:17 — "And nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter."

1Ki 7:18 — "And he made the pillars, and two rows round about upon the one network, to cover the chapiters that were upon the top, with pomegranates: and so did he for the other chapiter."

2Ch 4:12 — "To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars;"

2Ch 4:13 — "And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars."

Modern Corruption

Scripture spends four passages on ornament that bore no weight, because beauty in the house of God is not waste.

expand to see more

Jachin and Boaz upheld no roof. They stood before the porch as signs — He shall establish, in Him is strength — and their capitals were dressed with chain work and four hundred pomegranates. The Holy Spirit thought this worth recording twice, in Kings and again in Chronicles, with the counts. That is a rebuke to the utilitarian instinct in worship, which asks of every element what it accomplishes. Some things in the house of God are there to say something true about God, and saying it is the whole of their function.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the regulative principle governs the elements of worship, not the beauty of them. What God has commanded is required and what He has not commanded is not permitted — but within what He commands, Scripture never treats care, skill, and loveliness as suspect. Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit of God to cut stones and carve timber. A bare aesthetic is not a purer one, and the pomegranates on the wreaths are in the text on purpose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sarsar (H8331), chain work, wreathed work; gedilah (H1434), twisted threads, wreaths; kothereth (H3805), the chapiter or crown of a pillar.

expand to see more

Hebrew sarsar (H8331) — chain work, wreath; 1 Kings 7:17, 2 Chronicles 4:12.

Hebrew gedilah (H1434) — twisted threads, fringes, wreaths; Deuteronomy 22:12, 1 Kings 7:17.

Hebrew kothereth (H3805) — chapiter, capital of a pillar; 1 Kings 7:16, 2 Chronicles 4:12.

Hebrew rimmon (H7416) — pomegranate; 2 Chronicles 4:13, Exodus 28:33.

Hebrew sebakah (H7639) — network, lattice; 1 Kings 7:17, 2 Kings 25:17.

Usage

"“Wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters” — metal cordage, not garlands."

"“Four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths” — counted, and recorded twice."

"“Seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other” — the number of completeness."
